name: Ruy López Exchange Variation
summary: The Exchange Ruy López (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Bxc6 dxc6) trades on c6 to head for a favourable pawn-structure endgame.
intro: The Exchange Variation of the Ruy López arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Bxc6 dxc6. White voluntarily surrenders the bishop pair to double Black's queenside pawns, banking on a superior long-term pawn structure and a healthy kingside majority in the endgame. It is a strategically clear, low-theory way of playing for a small but durable positional edge.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Bxc6 dxc6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By capturing with 4.Bxc6 dxc6, White inflicts doubled pawns on Black's queenside and creates a favourable pawn majority on the kingside. In a pure king-and-pawn endgame White's four-against-three kingside majority can produce a passed pawn, whereas Black's four-against-three queenside majority is crippled by the doubled c-pawns and cannot. This structural imbalance is the entire point of the variation: White is content to trade queens and pieces, steering toward endgames where the healthier majority quietly tells. The plan is prophylactic and patient rather than aggressive.

In return Black receives real compensation in the form of the bishop pair and open lines, particularly the half-open d-file and the freed light-squared bishop. Black's central pawn mass and active pieces give genuine dynamic chances in the middlegame, and if the queens and minor pieces stay on the board the two bishops can become powerful. The strategic battle is therefore a classic contest of structure against activity: White wants simplification and a clean endgame, while Black wants to keep pieces on and exploit the bishops before the ending arrives.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The critical continuation is 5.O-O, when Black most often replies 5...f6, supporting the e5-pawn so that pieces can be developed without conceding the centre. A well-known alternative is 5...Bg4, pinning the f3-knight and again bolstering e5 indirectly, or 5...Qd6 and 5...Bd6 setups that hold the e5-point and prepare quick development and castling. White frequently meets these with d4, challenging the centre and inviting exchanges that bring the structural theme to the fore, or with a slower plan of Nbd2, Nc4, and pressure against e5.

A famous try is the direct 5.Nxe5, the so-called pawn-grab, but after 5...Qd4 or 5...Qg5 Black regains the pawn with active play, so most strong players prefer the positional 5.O-O. Whichever route is chosen, the recurring middlegame plans revolve around the same structural fight: White manoeuvres to trade into the ending and mobilise the kingside majority, while Black uses the bishops and open lines to generate activity and keep the position complex. Because the resulting positions are strategically rich but not sharply forcing, the Exchange has long been favoured by players seeking a solid, understanding-based game.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Exchange Variation has been part of Ruy López theory since the nineteenth century, but it gained its greatest prestige when Emanuel Lasker used it as a practical, low-risk weapon to grind down strong opposition, and it was later revived at the highest level by Bobby Fischer, who demonstrated its venom in several celebrated games. Its appeal lies in reducing the vast theory of the Spanish to a handful of clear structural ideas, making it a favourite of positional players who relish squeezing small endgame advantages. It remains a respected and fully sound way to sidestep the heavily analysed Closed Ruy López.

keyIdeas: 4.Bxc6 dxc6 doubles Black's c-pawns and hands White the bishop pair as compensation.
White's kingside pawn majority can make a passed pawn; Black's crippled majority cannot.
White aims to simplify and reach a favourable pure pawn endgame.
Black gets the two bishops, the half-open d-file, and central activity.
The core battle is structure and simplification versus activity and complexity.
A clear, low-theory way to sidestep the deeply analysed Closed Ruy López.

white: Trade pieces and queens to reach an endgame where the structure tells.
Advance the kingside pawn majority to create a passed pawn.
Play d4 at the right moment to open the position and force exchanges.
Restrain Black's bishop pair and avoid opening lines prematurely.
Manoeuvre knights to strong central squares and pressure the e5-pawn.
black: Support the e5-pawn with ...f6 or ...Bg4 to keep the centre intact.
Develop the bishops actively and exploit the half-open d-file.
Keep pieces on the board to make the two bishops count.
Use the central pawn majority to seize space and generate play.
Avoid mass simplification into a bad pawn ending.
